headline: Rates Ease to Two-Week Low Amid Stock Slide
tileReason: Bond markets are closed today for Thanksgiving; on Wednesday, the latest trading day, the daily 30-year average fell to 7.26%, a two-week low, as nervous investors moved from stocks into bonds.
takeaway:
Bond markets are closed today for Thanksgiving, so today's numbers come from Wednesday, the most recent trading day. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average fell to 7.26% Wednesday from 7.32% Tuesday, another two-week low. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, released a day early on Wednesday, dropped to 7.21% from 7.28%, and the Mortgage Research Center showed about 7.10%.

Falling stocks pulled money into bonds again. Tech shares sold off sharply early Wednesday before recovering part of the loss, and nervous investors bought Treasuries for safety, which pushes yields down. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, ended the day near 4.85% to 4.86%, down about 0.05% to 0.07%, its eighth straight daily decline. Mortgage bond prices rose about 0.29 point, which lets lenders offer lower rates.

Bonds shrugged off a batch of strong reports. Third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3% from 3.4%, and first-time jobless claims fell to 189,000, both signs of a sturdy economy that would normally push rates up. The Fed's preferred inflation measure, PCE, rose 3.8% from a year earlier, and the core version, which leaves out food and energy, rose 3.3%, a tenth above forecasts. The yield decline started before these reports came out, so they didn't drive the move.

The Fed's Beige Book, a roundup of business conditions around the country, was mixed. Eight of the 12 Fed districts reported slight to moderate growth and four reported no change, while businesses said prices were still rising at a moderate pace and expect costs to keep climbing. New home sales jumped about 14% in October, though that report is often revised a lot.

A December Fed hike is still seen as nearly certain. Futures markets (where traders bet on the Fed's next move) put the odds of a quarter-point increase on Dec 9 at about 98% Wednesday, with about 2% on no change. Readings for another hike in January range from roughly 40% to 60%. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast.

Lenders still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room is part of why lenders have been able to pass along recent bond rallies.

Bond markets reopen Friday for a shortened session that closes at 2 PM ET, and holiday trading is often thin and choppy. After that, the big tests are the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

drivers.title: Stock slide sends money into bonds
drivers.text: Tech stocks fell sharply early Wednesday, with the Nasdaq down as much as about 4.6% before recovering part of the loss. Nervous investors buy Treasuries for safety, which lowers yields; the 10-year ended near 4.86%, its eighth straight daily drop, and mortgage bond prices rose.

drivers.title: Core inflation runs a bit hot
drivers.text: October's core PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, rose 3.3% from a year earlier, a tenth above forecasts and up from 3.1%. Hotter inflation usually pushes yields up because it keeps the Fed raising rates, but bonds largely looked past it.

drivers.title: December Fed hike nearly locked in
drivers.text: Futures odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec 9 are about 98%, and markets see a real chance of another in January. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling far.

drivers.title: Economy still looks strong
drivers.text: Third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3%, and first-time jobless claims fell to 189,000. A strong economy can keep inflation sticky, which tends to hold rates up, though bonds rallied anyway on Wednesday.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap gives lenders room to pass along bond rallies.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 25 close (latest trading day; markets closed Nov 26 for Thanksgiving)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even. Rates are at a two-week low after eight straight days of falling Treasury yields, and the gap between mortgage rates and Treasuries is still wide (about 2.19% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), which leaves room for lenders to cut. Working against borrowers: core inflation came in a bit hot, growth and the job market still look strong, a December Fed hike is all but priced in, and after a long rally yields can bounce back. Big swing events: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and its projections, Dec 10 consumer prices, the stock market and oil headlines.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

calendar.why: Consumers' inflation expectations feed into the Fed's thinking, and Fed comments about more hikes can push rates up.
calendar.actual: 51.5; consumers expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down from 4.3% early this month, and 3.3% over five years
calendar.surpriseLabel: in line, with lower inflation expectations
calendar.reaction: Stocks fell 3.7% and the 10-year yield dropped about 0.12% to near 4.92%, and lenders cut mortgage rates during the day.

calendar.label: Mon, Nov 23
calendar.event: November business surveys (S&P Global flash PMIs); $69B 2-year note sale; New York Fed President Williams speaks
calendar.why: Williams is one of the Fed's most influential voices, so any hint about the pace of hikes can move rates.
calendar.actual: Williams said inflation near 3.5% is too high and he wouldn't rule out back-to-back hikes; 2-year notes sold at about 4.70%; Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and the S&P 500 jumped 4.7%
calendar.reaction: The 10-year yield jumped early on the stock rally, then settled about unchanged near 4.92% as oil fell; mortgage rates edged up 0.01%.

calendar.why: Strong confidence points to a sturdy economy and spending, which tends to push rates up.
calendar.actual: 103.3, highest since January 2025; Case-Shiller 20-city home prices +2.6% from a year earlier (2.7% expected); 5-year notes sold at 4.719%
calendar.reaction: Bonds held up as tech stocks fell; the 10-year ended near 4.91% and the 30-year mortgage average slipped 0.02% to 7.32%.

calendar.label: Wed, Nov 25

calendar.why: Hotter inflation would add to the case for more Fed hikes and push rates up.
calendar.actual: PCE 0.3% monthly (3.8% yearly); core 0.3% (3.3% yearly); Q3 growth revised to 4.3% from 3.4%; jobless claims 189K, down 13K; durable goods orders +0.2%; new home sales 701K pace, up 14.2%; MBA 30-year 7.38%, purchase applications +10%; Freddie Mac 30-year 7.21%; Beige Book: 8 of 12 districts growing slightly to moderately, prices still rising moderately
calendar.reaction: Yields fell anyway, a move that began before the reports as tech stocks slid; the 10-year ended near 4.86%, mortgage bond prices rose about 0.29 and the 30-year mortgage average fell 0.06% to 7.26%.

talkingPoints.buyers: Mortgage rates fell to a two-week low on Wednesday, with the daily 30-year average at 7.26% and Freddie Mac's weekly survey at 7.21%. Bond markets are closed for Thanksgiving, and a December Fed hike still looks nearly certain with inflation sticky, so the picture can change quickly after the holiday. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates are at their lowest in two weeks, around 7.26%, and purchase mortgage applications jumped about 10% last week. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out over the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates slipped to a two-week low near 7.26% heading into Thanksgiving as a stock slide pulled investors into bonds.
